title: Warmer seas and shifting pressure systems: the signs that suggest the Mediterranean’s climate is ‘tropicalising’
content:
Nowhere in the Iberian Peninsula or the Balearic Islands has a tropical climate – for this to be the case, the average temperature in the coldest month would have to be 18°C or higher. The contrast between Spain’s winters and summers, and the low temperatures reached in winter, do not resemble those of any tropical climate.

However, over recent decades, climates across Mediterranean basin have begun to show signs of tropicalisation: the process of transitioning towards a tropical climate.

This is evident in several areas, including rising air and sea temperatures, shifting atmospheric patterns, and increasingly erratic rainfall.

Firstly, a marked rise in air temperature – more pronounced than the global average – is making the Mediterranean’s winters shorter and its summers longer, bringing spring forward and delaying the onset of autumn. Some people believe that these transitional seasons have all but disappeared. They do still exist, but they have moved on the calendar.

Leer más: Summers are getting longer each year, and it isn’t all fun and games

The temperature of shallow and deep Mediterranean water – down to a depth of around 100m – has also risen markedly.

title: Lula wins a ‘miracle’ election in Brazil. Now comes the hard part: putting the country back on the right track
content:
Three weeks ago, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s political obituaries had all been written.

The far-right presidential candidate, Flávio Bolsonaro, son of the jailed former President Jair Bolsonaro, had come out of the first round of the presidential election with a lead that looked impossible to overcome.

At 80 years old, Lula seemed headed for a quiet exit after four decades at the centre of Brazilian political life.

On Sunday, however, Lula proved everyone wrong. He won the runoff and secured a fourth non-consecutive term as Brazil’s president.

The election result is unprecedented in Brazilian politics in at least three ways.

First, no Brazilian presidential candidate had ever won the first round and then lost the runoff. Since the two-round system was adopted by the 1988 Brazilian Constitution, the first-round leader had always gone on to win.

Lula broke that pattern by turning a defeat of around 2.2 million votes in the first round into a solid victory, in three weeks.
snippet: Three weeks ago, Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s political obituaries had all been written.
creator: Guilherme Casarões, Associate Professor of Brazilian Studies, Florida International University

title: US midterms: what a new Congress could – and could not – change for Europe
content:
US midterm elections traditionally attract fewer voters than presidential contests. But this year’s vote is drawing considerable attention at home and abroad, especially in Europe.

Europe has not even needed to wait for the election results to feel their impact. With fuel prices weighing on American voters, Donald Trump has recently reached a deal to start importing Russian diesel in the hope of lowering fuel prices before election day. It was a stunning reversal of years of US pressure on Moscow over its war against Ukraine.

The contrast with Europe is striking. On October 12, the EU adopted its largest single expansion of sanctions against Russia’s military-industrial complex, targeting 1,569 individuals and entities. Four days later, Trump waived major new US sanctions on Russia, under legislation he had signed just a few weeks before.

These decisions send an uncomfortable message to Kyiv and European capitals: pressure on Russia is not a given, and can be relaxed when US electoral interests take priority.

With Republican losses looking increasingly likely, US Congress could look very different in a few weeks. But could a new Congress change US-Europe relations?

title: French students are showing us what protest looks like in the age of viral spectacle
content:
The recent wave of protests in Europe have left us with two striking, viral spectacles of violence and joy. As Limoges’ historic town hall went up in flames, the Orchestre du Nouveau Monde was playing classical music in Paris’ central Place de la République (until the musicians were teargassed by police, that is).

Both scenes offer radically different ways of seeing the protests. The burning town hall offers a powerful image of destruction; the orchestra, of anti-authoritarian collective solidarity. Neither tells the whole story, but their contrast raises important questions: which image will come to represent the protests, and who decides what we see?

France’s demonstrations began with students protesting deteriorating school conditions, including staff shortages and dilapidated buildings. But they quickly intersected with broader anger over living costs and public services.

The unrest also formed part of a wider European moment. On the same weekend, people took to the streets in Spain, Italy, Belgium, Portugal and Albania. Grievances include low wages, rising energy prices and unaffordable housing, each within its own national context.

title: France’s ‘casseurs’: why the term fails to do justice to the extent of looting and spiralling unrest
content:
Following widespread looting sprees and acts of violence occurring on the sidelines of the October 17 student protests, so-called “casseurs” seem to be the centre of attention. But the term, which comes from the French verb casser or “to break”, poses more questions than answers. The sociologist Paolo Stuppia examines the unprecedented situation many cities across France are having to contend with, and the complex combination of collective action whose motivations are unclear and the social media’s extreme agility.

The Conversation: How unprecedented are the scenes of looting that we witnessed on the sidelines of the October 17 demonstrations?

Paolo Stuppia: What may be unprecedented is the extent of the destruction of private property and the goods that have been stolen. It should be clear, however, that not all the looters can necessarily be sorted into identifiable groups, at least politically.

title: Elderly women are often victims of gender-based violence. Why is it so hard for them to get help?
content:
In 1997, Ana Orantes appeared on an Andalusian television programme to recount a lifetime of abuse at the hands of her husband. Just a few days after her harrowing testimony, she was brutally murdered by her abuser. Her case prompted a widespread reckoning on gender-based violence in Spain, which led to significant legislative reforms.

Ana Orantes died at the age of 60 as an elderly woman who had suffered violence and abuse for 40 years. But today, despite the impact that her case had, older victims of gender-based violence remain marginalised, to the point of being practically invisible. They do not fit the social stereotype of a victim, which we tend to associate with a young woman, often with young children in her care.

But while gender-based violence affects all kinds of women, of all ages and from all walks of life, not all victims find themselves in the same circumstances. And for any intervention to work, it must take this complex reality into account.

Elder gender-based abuse often merges two realities: domestic violence stretching back years or decades, and abuse of older people associated with dependence and care, often in the form of neglect or psychological abuse.

title: Is France in 2026, Greece in 2009?
content:
France’s ten-year government bond yield reached 5% last week, its highest level in more than two decades. The extra interest it pays over Germany – the “spread” investors use to gauge French-specific risk – has widened dramatically. Parliament is wrestling with a 2027 budget requiring €54 billion in fiscal measures, while protests and violent clashes across France dominate the headlines.

With political instability and social tensions rising, comparisons with Greece at the start of its debt crisis have become inevitable. As Greece’s finance minister when its crisis erupted in 2009, I am increasingly asked how the two situations compare. I understand the temptation, but also how misleading it can be.

France is not Greece. It is one of the world’s largest economies, with globally competitive companies, substantial household savings, a deep financial system, robust institutions. And, unlike Greece in 2009, it has no large external financing imbalance.

title: New long-clawed British dinosaur is the first of its kind in Europe
content:
The fossilised skull of a new species of mysterious meat-eating dinosaur from the Isle of Wight has been rediscovered in the collections of the Natural History Museum after over 100 years in storage.

Over its nearly 150-year history, this London museum has become home to over 30 million specimens, making it fairly easy to forget about the odd fossil or rock here and there. This is almost definitely what happened to the only known fossil of the UK’s newest dinosaur, a two-legged meat-eating theropod (the dinosaur family including birds) which we have named Invictibellatrix amberina in a new study.

title: Is it better to vaccinate against COVID and flu together, or separately?
content:
As autumn sets in and temperatures fall across the northern hemisphere, vaccination campaigns are getting underway. Vaccination is not just the most effective way to prevent severe forms of infection and avoid hospital admissions – it also protects health systems, preventing them from becoming overburdened when annual case numbers reach their peak.

The viruses that cause flu and COVID are constantly evolving, meaning we gradually lose any immunity we have acquired over time. The vaccines used in each campaign are therefore specifically formulated and adapted each year, in response to the most recent variants identified by the World Health Organization’s global surveillance and monitoring networks.

Contrary to popular belief, the primary aim of vaccination programmes is not to prevent infection. Instead, they aim to reduce the severity of the disease, the risk of hospitalisation, admission to intensive care units, and deaths among those at higher risk of complications.

title: The mafia isn’t keeping fentanyl out of Europe – the lack of demand is
content:
Fentanyl and other synthetic opioids are still the single biggest driver of overdose deaths in the US. They were involved in around 38,000 of the roughly 70,000 deaths recorded in 2025, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Europe’s figures are of a different order. In 16 countries that reported data, fentanyl and its derivatives were linked to a total of around 210 drug-induced deaths in 2024, up from about 130 in 2023. Most of that rise may involve medicines rather than illicitly made fentanyl.

Other potent synthetic opioids, notably nitazenes, have driven recent peaks in deaths in several countries. In Italy, the government’s latest report on addiction counted only five fentanyl-related deaths in 2025.

This gap has prompted a striking explanation: that Italy’s mafias, wary of a drug that kills their customers and draws police attention, have chosen to keep fentanyl out.

It is a compelling story. But it does not fit what we know about drug markets or mafias. Europe’s comparatively low fentanyl numbers are better explained by something less cinematic: there is very little demand for it.

title: The little-known 14th century battle that has shaped English, Scottish and French relations
content:
On October 17, 1346, the battle of Neville’s Cross was fought outside Durham in the north-east of England. It was a decisive moment in Anglo-Scottish history that led to the capture of King David II of Scotland. Yet few have heard of it.

Other battles are far better known. Those of Stirling Bridge (1297), Falkirk (1298) and Bannockburn (1314) are more famous because of the exploits of William Wallace and Robert the Bruce. Similarly well-known are the successes of Edward III, the Black Prince and Henry V at Crécy (1346), Poitiers (1356) and Agincourt (1415), respectively.

Yet, less than two months after Crécy, a decisive victory was won in northern England. The battle of Neville’s Cross remains one of the least publicly known but decisive battles in English history.

As Edward III gathered a force of 15,000 men to invade France in 1346, King Philip VI of France requested Scottish aid. He wrote to King David in June and again in July: “I implore you to remember our friendship and our treaties and to strike as hard at England as you can.”

With Edward III and most of his nobles in France, Philip reassured David that England was a “defenceless void”. The opportunity was too good to miss.

title: Maricarmen Abascal: how a disabled, evicted 87-year-old woman became a political football in Spain’s upcoming election
content:
In Spain, an average of 44 evictions are carried out every day. While statistics like this are shocking, numbers alone rarely spark a revolution. Mass protest movements instead tend to rally around one compelling individual story.

This was exactly what happened with 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal, who has become so famous that she is known in Spain as simply Maricarmen. Following an insurmountable rent hike and a lengthy legal battle, she was evicted from her Madrid home of 71 years in September, and died on October 7. She quickly become a household name, and the figurehead of Spain’s housing protests.

Her case stirred the empathy of millions, and inspired collective shame that society was unable to prevent an elderly woman from being forced out of her home on a stretcher. Her story made headlines around the world, sparked a wave of fierce, nationwide protests, and led to an unravelling of Spanish politics that has culminated in a snap election on November 29 and a general strike planned for November 11.

title: How one of the world’s biggest music stars is transforming the Spanish language
content:
According to the Royal Spanish Academy (RAE, under its Spanish acronym), a “piquete” is either a sharp object, a small wound, or a group of striking workers blocking access to a workplace. It is a word, generally speaking, of conflict and harm.

But when Puerto Rican musician Benito Antonio Martínez Ocasio – more commonly known as Bad Bunny – intones on his song NUEVAYoL “Tú tiene’ piquete mami, yo también” (“You’ve got piquete mami, and so do I”), he is not talking about trade unions or pointy sticks. He is referring to something else altogether, a way of moving through the world with a certain self confidence, attitude and style.

In Puerto Rico’s boricua dialect, the meaning of piquete is totally divorced from the RAE’s official uses. But unapologetic use of his native dialect is what defines the music of the world’s biggest Spanish-language musician.

Bad Bunny has put Spanish on more global stages than any other artist in recent history, yet he is also widely criticised for his way of speaking. This is rife on social media, where users complain that he “doesn’t talk properly”, he is “deforming the language”, and “doesn’t enunciate clearly”.

title: French school protests: a rite of passage – and the result of genuine concerns
content:
Across France, school students have taken to the streets to protest about teacher shortages, dilapidated school buildings and long school days.

While the tradition of student protest has long roots in France, the country’s current fiscal crisis combined with entrenched structural problems with teacher recruitment, sickness absence and a backlog of school maintenance means this is unlikely to be something the current government can easily address.

Problems – and protests – regarding conditions in French schools go back decades.

I’ve spent 20 years conducting research in France and protest has been a recurring theme. Many research participants I’ve worked with have spoken with fondness about protesting as high school students.

One participant in Nanterre, who went on to become a community activist, repeatedly spoke about how schools in poor Paris suburbs were institutions that would “crush you”. This was due in part to French educational culture, but also because of their under-resourcing and poor state of repair. To them protest felt like an outlet for these grievances.

title: How the ‘geopolitical stigma’ associated with Putin’s Russia is affecting ordinary Russians
content:
Russia’s international standing collapsed within weeks of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Sanctions swept across Russian banks, businesses and political elites, while western companies exited the country en masse. For those living inside Russia, it was the everyday, tangible shifts that made this feel real.

Western goods disappeared from supermarket shelves, direct flights to Europe stopped and getting visas to travel abroad became more difficult. Russian athletes, artists and scholars, meanwhile, were excluded from international competitions, cultural platforms and academic events.

For Russians living elsewhere in Europe, the change was often more subtle. Questions about their nationality in job applications, negative media coverage and offhand comments about Russia all contributed to a growing sense that being Russian now meant carrying a stigma. Russia’s changing international reputation had suddenly become personal.

title: Inside two prison systems: why Denmark and the UK punish so differently
content:
It has been said that a society should be judged not by how it treats its outstanding citizens but by how it treats people who break the law.

I research prisons and am interested in what incarceration reveals about the relationship between the state and the people in its care.

By this standard, the UK and Denmark tell very different stories. In 2025, Denmark’s prison population stood at around 69 people per 100,000 residents, compared with about 170 per 100,000 in the UK – roughly one and a half times higher.

One way to understand this difference is through welfare. With its wide range of universal welfare state services such as heavily subsidised daycare, free healthcare, free education and high standards of public services, Denmark’s criminal justice system has traditionally placed greater emphasis on rehabilitation and reintegration. Prisoners retain the right to vote, maintain closer contact with family and are generally encouraged to participate in ordinary social life where possible.

title: China and the EU could turn Morocco into a surprise global hub for electric vehicles
content:
China now makes more than seven in ten of the world’s electric cars. In 2024 it produced over 12 million, 1.25 million of which were exported, mainly to Europe.

The EU is worried about this – alarmed by cheap, state-subsidised Chinese vehicles flooding its market and threatening the 13 million jobs which depend on its own auto industry. So the bloc has spent the past two years building a system of tariffs and rules to keep Chinese cars at bay.

In 2024, it imposed extra duties of up to 35% on Chinese electric vehicles (EVs), on top of an existing 10% import tariff. So far though, the EU’s tactics have yielded limited results.

Chinese vehicle sales in Europe nearly doubled between 2024 and 2025.

And much of this sales volume is being driven by the EV powerhouse that is developing at speed in Morocco.

Chinese firms producing cars in Morocco avoid exposure to those EU tariffs, and have announced US$6 billion (£4.5 billion) of investment in battery and electric car component plants in the country.

title: Donald Trump aligns with Vladimir Putin yet again, leaving Ukraine – and US relations with Europe – under pressure
content:
The deal struck by Donald Trump with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, on October 9 to allow Russia to sell millions of tonnes of diesel is a major departure from US policy and runs counter to Ukrainian and European interests. It also directly contradicts a law signed by the US president in September to authorise fresh US sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas.

The timing of this deal was unfortunate. A senior Ukrainian and European delegation were in Miami for talks with Trump’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. On the table were apparently new US proposals which included a pre-winter de-escalation in the four-and-a-half-year war.

Once in the room, the US envoys reportedly signalled that sanctions relief on Russia was coming. But this still left Ukrainian and European officials blindsided by the announcement. Unsurprisingly, the talks ended the same day without any agreement and a day earlier than planned.

title: Women are more emotionally intelligent than men, and that’s a problem – landmark study
content:
Who comes to mind when you think of someone emotionally intelligent? Someone who can read a room, defuse an argument, and who knows exactly what to say when a friend is struggling? For many people, that person is a woman. It’s such a widely held belief that popular psychology treats it as fact.

We decided to put that assumption to the test. Our new study, co-led by Dr Vera Hampel and co-authored with Leon Bach, reviewed nearly three decades of research, from 1995 to 2023, across 76 countries and more than 600,000 people. We wanted to answer a simple question: are women really more emotionally intelligent than men? The headline answer is yes, on average, women score higher.

But the more useful finding is the type of emotional intelligence women seem to excel at, and what it potentially costs the people who have it.

Emotional intelligence is the ability to recognise, understand and regulate emotions in yourself and in others. When we looked at each element of emotional intelligence, the female advantage turned out to be concentrated in the “others’ feelings” half of the equation.

title: French student protests: comparisons with 1968 will only serve the political extremes
content:
The student demonstrations that have spread across France in recent weeks are not unprecedented. Indeed, commentators have been quick to point to comparisons with the events of May and June 1968, where, at their peak, more than 10 million students and workers took to the streets.

In 1968, as now, there were legitimate reasons for protest. The unrest began at the Nanterre campus of the University of Paris, which was miles from the city centre and poorly equipped for the changing social norms of the 1960s. In particular, the ban on women and men being able to enter each other’s accommodation was the catalyst for initial demonstrations that then spread into central Paris and beyond.

Today’s parallels with the past are unmistakable. What began in September as a demonstration at the poor quality of high school (lycée) buildings in the Parisian suburbs (this time Saint-Denis) has escalated into wider protests about the conditions facing young people in France today.

title: How Spain’s torrential rainstorms put sewage into its rivers and seas
content:
After heavy rain, Spanish cities often awaken to refreshed air and clean streets, while the rainwater itself vanishes into storm drains along with everything it swept away. Under the ground, however, a very different story unfolds.

Once rainwater enters the sewerage network, it mixes with domestic waste water: everything that goes down shower, kitchen and bathroom drains, and toilets. This water carries fecal matter and bacteria, along with toilet paper, cleaning products, and many, other things.

If everything works as it should, these waters flow through sewerage pipes into treatment centres. The wastewater leaves these centres much cleaner than it came in, and is discharged into rivers and seas.

But, in the words of Valencian singer Raimon: “In my land, the rain doesn’t know how to rain. It rains too much, or too little. If it rains too little: drought. If it rains too much: catastrophe.”

He has been proven right several times in recent years, from Barcelona’s Nova Icària beach to the Valencian coast after the devastating floods of October 2024. While the Valencia floods were exceptionally powerful and deadly, extreme rainfall is becoming increasingly common in Spain.

title: Spain’s snap election: will Pedro Sánchez’s latest gamble pay off?
content:
On October 5, Spain’s prime minister Pedro Sánchez called a snap general election for November 29, bringing the vote forward by 10 months.

One of the main advantages of being in government is the ability to shape the political agenda. Spain’s system also grants incumbent leaders the power to call (or not call) early elections. So why is Sánchez calling elections now?

On the face of it, it seems like like odd timing, as Sánchez’s Socialist party (the PSOE) and the government it leads have been under intense pressure for months.

The inner circles of both the PSOE and Sánchez himself have been dogged by years of corruption allegations. The crisis in Ceuta has added further pressure – it shifted the migration debate towards security and deportations, and away from Sánchez’s position of regularisation, employment and inclusion.

But recent events have placed housing front and centre. The eviction of Maricarmen Abascal – a disabled 87-year-old in Madrid whose rent was hiked by 230% after an investment fund bought her house – sparked protests across Spain, including encampments in major city centres.

title: What Europe’s EU Inc. framework for boosting competitiveness can and should learn from startup fraud in the US
content:
The European Parliament and the Council of the European Union are currently debating EU Inc, draft legislation seeking to establish a single set of rules for starting, operating, and growing a business across EU member states. The proposed framework is designed to make business registration and operation within the EU faster, easier, and more harmonised.

The proposed “28th regime” promises company registration within 48 hours for under €100 via fully digitalised procedures – including for raising capital and accessing the stock market, and simplified liquidation proceedings to make dissolving and relaunching a business more seamless. The proposal is part of the broader EU Startup and Scaleup Strategy, whose ambition is to narrow the innovation gap between the EU and its global competitors, notably the United States.

title: A camera combined with AI could help further diagnosis of movement disorders like spinal muscular atrophy in newborns
content:
Detecting impaired motor function as early as possible after birth with the help of a standard camera linked to intelligent systems can help in diagnosing infantile conditions characterised by hypotonia: reduction or loss of active muscle movement. A research team is investigating this approach based on the work carried out on babies with spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), a rare genetic neuromuscular disorder.

In 2019, the drug Zolgensma made headline news as the world’s most expensive treatment. The price of this medicine for spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) has been set at nearly 2 million euros per injection.

And, at the same time, what an extraordinary breakthrough! It promises to provide a definitive cure for a genetic disease that, if survivors do live, leads to extremely severe disabilities in children affected by what is the world’s first hereditary peripheral neurological disorder.

Behind these staggering figures lies an urgent medical situation. For these therapies to be effective, it is essential to identify the condition as early as possible. This is precisely the challenge our team set out to tackle, by using an ordinary camera coupled with artificial intelligence.

title: Nobel physics prize awarded for discovery of ‘ghostly messengers’ from the cosmos
content:
The 2026 Nobel prize for physics has been awarded to US-based researcher Francis Halzen for his discovery of high energy neutrino particles from space.

The Nobel committee said Halzen has made “decisive contributions” to the discovery of “neutrinos of astrophysical origin” with IceCube, an experiment installed under ice at the South Pole.

Ellen Moons, secretary general of the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, described these neutrinos as “ghostly messengers”. This references the fact the particles have nearly no mass and pass through solid objects with hardly any interaction. In fact, billions of neutrinos pass through any given person on Earth every second.

Most of these neutrinos are emitted by the Sun. However, high energy neutrinos coming from elsewhere in the cosmos also reach our planet. These neutrinos are about a billion times rarer than those that stream out from the Sun.

They originate from diverse sources, such as black holes located at the hearts of distant galaxies that accelerate particles to extreme energies.

title: October 7: a Palestinian-Israeli memoir seeks to break the cycle of violence
content:
Since the Hamas attacks of October 7, 2023, the world has witnessed unimaginable, almost constant violence in Gaza and the West Bank. But people’s understanding of these events is not universal – each person is exposed to a particular set of narratives surrounding history, victimhood and trauma.

The vast majority of news reports, social media posts, videos, and books that have covered the events since October 7, 2023 can be defined as what I call “conflict media”, which reproduces the divisions of the conflict it describes, perpetuating it to the point where the media itself becomes a weapon in an information war.

As a scholar of the Middle East, I have rarely – though not never – encountered conflict media’s opposite, which I call “resolution media”.

The most famous works of resolution media have emerged after a conflict ends, and highlight the universal suffering of war. Wilfred Owen’s first world war poem Dulce et Decorum Est, for instance, is still widely quoted to expose “the old Lie” that it is “sweet and fitting” to die for one’s country.

title: The UK and Denmark: a dentist assesses the state of the nations’ teeth
content:
Teeth are an unlikely place to start when judging a health system, but they can be one of the most revealing.

Oral health tells a surprisingly big story. Tooth decay, gum disease and tooth loss are some of the most common chronic conditions anywhere in the world, and they often reflect how seriously a health system takes prevention.

As a dentist and researcher, this is the part that always stays with me: oral disease is rarely about one bad tooth. It is usually about the system around that tooth. What is prevented early? What is picked up late? And who can get care without delay? That makes England and Denmark an interesting comparison. Both are wealthy European countries with strong welfare traditions, but their dental systems work in very different ways.

Health Gap / Sundhedskløften is a collaborative series from The Conversation UK and Denmark’s Videnskab.dk exploring what the two countries can learn from each other when it comes to health and wellbeing.

From cycling and alcohol to inequality, healthcare and everyday habits, the series looks beyond hospitals and medical treatment to explore how culture, politics and society shape the way people live – and how healthy they are.
snippet: Teeth are an unlikely place to start when judging a health system, but they can be one of the most revealing.

title: Optogenetics wins the Nobel – one neuroscience breakthrough in a line of technological innovations helping scientists map and control the brain
content:
The brain is unbelievably complicated, which is both daunting and fascinating for neuroscientists like me. In the space of a cubic millimeter – about the size of a single poppy seed – there are tens of thousands of neurons and other brain support cells, all influencing each other’s function.

How do neuroscientists make sense of this complexity? And how did they get to the point where they could simply shine different colors of light on the brain to control neuron activity?

The answer is one step at a time, with a lot of help from technology.

Revisiting some of the technological advances that have supported researchers’ current understanding of how the brain works can point to where the field of neuroscience might be going next. There is a rough pattern to the technological advances that have led neuroscience to the present day: visualize the brain, measure its function and then control it.

Using light to influence neuronal function, known as optogenetics, allows neuroscientists to manipulate what neurons do millisecond by millisecond. The researchers whose work led to this technique won the 2026 Nobel Prize in physiology or medicine.

title: Russia is using Ukraine’s children to win its occupation – and the wider war
content:
A year or so after the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the city of Murmansk in Russia’s Arctic north-west marked its annual regional day with a celebration for children. Alongside the sons and daughters of Russian soldiers stood children taken from the occupied Prymorskyi district of Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region.

Ukraine’s authorities have verified 20,651 cases of children deported or forcibly displaced to Russia and Belarus since 2022. Some estimates, including figures shared by Russian officials themselves, run as high as 744,000. As of September 2026, just 2,644 Ukrainian children have been returned.

The International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants for the Russian leader, Vladimir Putin, and his children’s commissioner, Maria Lvova-Belova, in March 2023 for their roles in this campaign.

But the Where Are Our People? project, which I work alongside, has identified at least 47 Russian and Belarusian individuals directly involved in the deportations. These people range from regional governors to business executives. Only some of them are under western sanctions.

title: One in three Ukrainian civilians estimated to meet the criteria for PTSD or complex PTSD – new study
content:
Resilience is a word frequently used to describe the way Ukrainian society has responded to the war with Russia. It’s a term that can inspire sympathy and mobilise support. But it also risks overshadowing effects of war that require both domestic and international attention to enable Ukraine to withstand Russia’s invasion and manage long-term recovery.

The protracted conflict that started with Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014, continued with the war in Donbas and escalated into Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022 has recently reached a new level of intensity through concerted Russian attacks on civilian targets. As a result, the effects of war at the level of individuals, communities and society at large are becoming ever more apparent.

Trauma is an unavoidable effect of war. Measuring the psychological effects of trauma in countries following war and conflict can be difficult. Obtaining a reliable picture of the situation in Ukraine – where, after four and a half years, there is no end to the conflict in sight – has proved even more challenging.

title: As Baltic states face Russian hybrid aggression, our research shows what Europe can do
content:
EU defence ministers assembled in Brussels on September 28 to try to formulate a response to increasing Russian aggression in Europe. The talks focused on Russia’s strategy of hybrid warfare – that is, hostile acts that fall below the threshold of actual war.

These tend to include sabotage, disinformation, airspace violations, political interference and cyberwarfare. One part of Europe that has become familiar with these kinds of actions in recent years are the Baltic states – Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania. Quite apart from being nervous because of their physical proximity to Russia, these countries have had to deal with regular acts of hybrid warfare for some years now.

These tactics fall into what is often called the “grey zone” – they generally fall shy of the criteria needed to invoke Nato’s Article 5 clause of mutual self defence, which considers an attack on one member state as an attack on all. The increased use of hybrid actions has intensified in recent years, and the question of how to react to these grey zone threats has become a matter for debate inside Nato. The agreement is that a “game-changing” cyberattack could theoretically merit such a move.

title: Spain’s housing crisis is a warning for all of Europe – rights mean nothing if they’re not enforced
content:
When Maricarmen Abascal, a disabled 87 year-old, was evicted from the Madrid home where she had lived for 71 years, hundreds of people gathered outside in an attempt to prevent it. She was eventually forcibly removed from the building, and taken to hospital on a stretcher.

Her eviction sparked a wave of protests (still ongoing at the time of writing) against a housing crisis that, for many, has endured since the 2008 crash.

Following a week of negotiations and widespread demonstrations, Maricarmen’s landlord – a private investment fund that had hiked her rent by 230% – agreed to let her return under a new eight-year tenancy with limited rent. She is expected to return home after leaving hospital.

But the protests that followed her eviction are not just about one woman’s story. They reflect a deeper problem that extends beyond Spain. Across Europe, countless others like Maricarmen are facing similar struggles to find and keep a roof over their heads.

In Spain, the contradiction is striking. Article 47 of Spain’s Constitution recognises the right to “decent and adequate” housing, and requires public authorities to create the “conditions necessary to make that right effective”.

title: How World Trade Organization reform could help address the EU-China trade imbalance
content:
The world was closely watching the high-stakes US-China summit in Washington from September 23 – 25, which resulted in the US and China agreeing, among other things, to extend their trade truce by two months. Now, the spotlight has shifted to Beijing, as the EU and China enter the final stretch ahead of a decisive round of trade talks seeking to remedy export/import imbalances. On October 8 and 9, trade negotiators from both sides will gather in Beijing for the second meeting of the newly established EU-China Trade and Investment Consultations Mechanism (TIC).

The TIC was launched in June this year, marking a significant step for both sides in restoring an institutional channel for dialogue on trade and investment after a period of relatively limited engagement. The forthcoming meeting is therefore more than a routine round of talks. It will be the first real test facing the new TIC: whether it is useful in stabilising EU-China relations and pulling the two back from the brink of a looming trade war. It is far too early to tell. What is already clear, however, is that some of the most difficult and pressing issues are on the negotiating table.

title: How do Denmark and the UK compare when it comes to alcohol and drinking habits?
content:
For decades, Denmark and the UK have been known as countries where alcohol plays a big role in people’s social lives. In this way, the two countries make an interesting comparison when it comes to alcohol consumption because they both have a strong drinking culture.

For years, Denmark has appeared near the top of European rankings for teenage alcohol use, with Danish teenagers consistently reporting higher levels of drinking than their peers in much of Europe — including the UK.

Binge drinking has historically been a particular concern in the UK, especially among young adults. But drinking habits have changed substantially since the 2000s, with the proportion of UK adults who reported binge drinking in the previous week falling from around 18% in 2005 to 15% in 2013.

In England, around 21% of adults drank more than 14 units of alcohol per week in 2024. This is equivalent to roughly six pints of average-strength beer or seven standard (175ml) glasses of wine. Denmark shows similar drinking rates.

title: Why Europe wants to boost its Arctic presence
content:
EU leaders gathered in northern Finland recently for a summit focused on reaffirming the importance of the Arctic region to European security. The meeting, which took place in the city of Rovaniemi, came a month before the EU is expected to release its updated Arctic policy.

This will be the first update since 2021, during which time the geopolitical climate has undergone considerable change. After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, for example, the work of the Arctic Council was put on hold.

The seven other Arctic states had previously used this forum to engage with Moscow directly, using it to exchange information and promote cooperation on issues such as environmental protection and development in the region.

Russia has stepped up its military, economic and strategic activities in the region over the intervening years.

On September 10, it was reported that a joint operation between the UK, US and Norway earlier in 2026 successfully disrupted Russian vessels simulating the deployment of a weapon designed to disable undersea cables near the remote Norwegian archipelago of Svalbard.

title: Water is precious – this Swedish city separates different waste sources to reuse more of it
content:
Extreme temperatures, droughts and wildfires lead to water scarcity and the search for alternative sources of water to secure supplies. With increasing pressures from climate change, Europe’s water stress – not having enough clean freshwater to meet demands – is becoming more intense and more frequent.

But one valuable water source is often overlooked: wastewater.

While some Middle Eastern countries like Qatar reuse approximately 90% of their wastewater, Europe’s reuse of wastewater is often very low. Just 0.6% of wastewater gets recycled in Sweden, yet 15 of 21 counties already face a high risk of water scarcity.

In one of those 15 counties, a new district in the city of Helsingborg in southern Sweden is successfully recycling wastewater. In Oceanhamnen, wastewater is collected through three separate pipelines: one for toilet wastewater (blackwater), one for greywater (wastewater from bathtubs and showers, sinks, laundry and dishwashers), and a third pipeline which takes food waste from the kitchen sink directly into biogas production.

title: Greater job security can make inventors less creative
content:
When Apple recently presented its (rather pricey) new folding phone, one of the questions hovering over the launch – and in particular its new CEO, John Ternus – was whether the technology giant can recover its famously innovative magic touch.

Apple remains extraordinarily profitable, but the company that revolutionised consumer electronics in the 2000s has been dogged by concerns over its dependency on a single, decades-old product – the iPhone – and its associated services. There is intense speculation around whether Ternus will reinvigorate the culture of radical innovation that drove Apple’s growth, as well as the development of the smartphone itself.

But concerns around innovation are not confined to one tech company. Over the last few months, figures like Gordon Brown and Ursula von der Leyen have underscored its vital economic importance, as well as its glaring absence from European industry in particular.

title: Without water, forests lose their ability to absorb CO₂
content:
To survive during periods of drought, trees halt photosynthesis, a highly water-intensive process during which, for every molecule of CO₂ absorbed by a tree leaf, an average of around 400 water molecules are released. Entire forests then may end up emitting more CO₂ than they capture.

This is alarming given that droughts are becoming increasingly frequent and that forests play a key role in climate change mitigation policies. Although quantifying the CO₂ captured by the world’s forests remains a difficult task. It is estimated that they capture around a quarter of the CO₂ emitted by human activities.

However, when faced with extreme water shortages, forests can cease to act as carbon sinks. To understand why, we need to look at the leaves of the trees.

Tree leaves are the main point of entry for CO₂ into the forest ecosystem. They act as genuine chemical factories, capturing solar energy to convert CO₂ that is present in the air into sugar (i.e. photosynthesis). These sugars meet the plant’s energy needs. They also enable trees to grow and, in doing so, to store more CO₂ emitted by human activities.

title: Xenia Fedorova, or how Russian propaganda turns free thinking on itself
content:
KEY TAKEAWAYS

• On September 24, the European Union sanctioned Xenia Fedorova, the Russian former head of the French arm of Russia Today (RT) and media commentator for the Bolloré group for her role in engaging in foreign information manipulation and interference (FIMI). It follows a French expulsion order against the Russian propagandist in July 2026.

• Accused of spreading Kremlin propaganda, she counterattacks by presenting herself as the victim of “single-minded thinking” spread by mainstream media in Western countries.

• In doing so, she exploits a clever rhetorical and cognitive mechanism: rather than trying to convince us, the aim is to turn our own aspiration to critical thinking against “official” sources, to push Russian propaganda.

The European Council has decided to adopt restrictive measures against Xenia Fedorova for her role in Russia’s continued hybrid activities, and in particular for engaging in foreign information manipulation and interference (FIMI), “thereby undermining democracy and stability in the EU and its member states”.
